G1 Academy

G1 Humanoid Academy

Native Unitree SDK & DDS development for the Unitree G1

A hands-on, four-day program: rebuild every abstraction sdk_wrapper.py provides — natively, one task at a time — ending in a perception-based pick-and-place capstone.

Course Intro 1 · Welcome

Welcome to the Humanoid Academy

This academy teaches you to program the Unitree G1 humanoid directly against its native interfaces — the Unitree Python SDK (unitree_sdk2py) and the DDS messages/topics underneath it — rather than only calling a pre-built convenience wrapper.

  • By the end, you will have rebuilt, piece by piece, everything academy/sdk_wrapper.py's G1 class provides: DDS setup, state observation, mode switching, locomotion, SLAM, arm/hand control, and a perception-based delivery pipeline.
  • Every task ends with your code landing in your own notebook, checked against a reference solution, and reusable via solved/lib_solved.py for the next task.
  • Goal: leave knowing exactly what a convenience method like g1.say(...) or g1.ik_move_ee(...) does underneath, so you can debug it, extend it, or build your own.

Course Intro 9 · G1 hardware (1/3)

G1 hardware (1/3): 29 degrees of freedom

The G1's body is a 29-joint array, addressed everywhere in this course by a fixed integer index — the same index order the low-level rt/lowstate/rt/lowcmd messages use.

  • Legs (12 joints, idx 0–11): hip pitch/roll/yaw, knee, ankle pitch/roll × 2 sides.
  • Waist (3 joints, idx 12–14): yaw, roll, pitch — roll/pitch are locked/absent on some waist-locked hardware variants.
  • Arms (14 joints, idx 15–28): shoulder pitch/roll/yaw, elbow, wrist roll/pitch/yaw × 2 sides.
  • Hands (Dex3, 7 joints/hand, not in the 29-DOF array): thumb (3 DOF) + two 2-DOF fingers, on their own rt/dex3/<side>/cmd topic — or Inspire hands as an alternative end effector.

Course Intro 12 · ROS 2

Intro to ROS 2

ROS 2 (this academy: Foxy) is a pub/sub + services + actions middleware for robotics: independent nodes exchange typed messages on named topics, with no node needing to know who else is listening.

  • Unitree runs its own DDS layer (via unitree_sdk2py's ChannelPublisher/ChannelSubscriber) on top of the same CycloneDDS transport ROS 2 uses — with RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp, a DDS topic rt/<name> and a ROS 2 topic /<name> are the same wire data.
  • Most tasks in this course use unitree_sdk2py's Channel API directly (no rclpy node needed) — it is simpler for one-off scripts/notebooks.
  • The bonus ROS 2 package track (and the cmd_vel → LocoClient bridge) uses rclpy nodes/publishers/subscribers directly, for when you need a long-running ROS 2 node instead of a notebook cell.
A real `ros2 topic list` terminal session — this is what the note below should show once ROS 2 is actually reachable.
Check ROS 2 is reachable: `source /opt/ros/foxy/setup.bash && ros2 topic list` should show `rt/...`-derived Unitree topics as `/...`.
Course Intro 13 · Unitree SDK

The Unitree Python SDK (unitree_sdk2py)

Every native call in this course goes through unitree_sdk2py: DDS channel setup, IDL message types, and high-level request/response clients.

  • ChannelFactoryInitialize(domain_id, iface) → ChannelPublisher/ChannelSubscriber for topics like rt/lowstate, rt/lowcmd, rt/dex3/*/cmd.
  • Typed IDL messages live under unitree_sdk2py.idl.unitree_hg (humanoid: LowState_, LowCmd_, HandCmd_, HandState_, ...) and unitree_sdk2py.idl.unitree_go (shared/quadruped-origin types like SportModeState_).
  • High-level request/response clients: LocoClient, MotionSwitcherClient, AudioClient, RobotStateClient, G1ArmActionClient — each wraps the generic unitree_sdk2py.rpc.client.Client RPC mechanism used directly in Task 7's SLAM client.
  • Reference: Unitree's own official examples are vendored in this repo at dev/old_scripts/arm_motion/g1_arm7_sdk_dds_example.py and sdk_details.md — read those alongside Tasks 8–9.
Transport dependency: unitree_sdk2py's DDS layer is built on Eclipse CycloneDDS — install/build it before the SDK (next slide).
Course Intro 14 · Environment setup

Environment setup

Get a clean, reproducible toolchain before touching the robot: Python → CycloneDDS → unitree_sdk2py, wired together by a couple of environment variables.

  1. Install a matching Python version for the target SDK/ROS 2 distro (this repo's Jetson image runs ROS 2 Foxy).
  2. Build/install CycloneDDS (the DDS implementation the SDK links against) and note its install prefix.
  3. Install unitree_sdk2py (pip install -e <path-to-unitree_sdk2_python>).
  4. Set PATH/LD_LIBRARY_PATH so the CycloneDDS shared libraries are found at import time.
  5. Export the environment variables below in every shell/kernel before running SDK code.
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp
export CYCLONEDDS_URI=/home/unitree/cyclonedds_ws/cyclonedds.xml
# CycloneDDS lib path, if not already on the default loader path:
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$CYCLONEDDS_HOME/lib:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH"
Hint — where to startRun `academy/setup_python_cyclonedds_unitree_sdk_.sh` for a scripted version of this checklist, then verify with `python3 -c "import unitree_sdk2py, cyclonedds; print('ok')"`.
Course Intro 15 · Network setup

Ethernet/IP: the Unitree subnet

The G1's onboard devices and your laptop all live on one private Ethernet subnet, 192.168.123.0/24. Every ChannelFactoryInitialize(domain_id, iface) call in this course needs iface set to the NIC joined to this subnet.

IPDeviceRole
192.168.123.164Jetson (onboard compute)runs the robot-side ROS 2 / DDS stack — the endpoint your SDK client actually talks to
192.168.123.120Livox Mid-360 LiDARpublishes the raw lidar cloud SLAM consumes
192.168.123.161Main board (robot controller)publishes rt/lowstate, accepts rt/lowcmd/rt/arm_sdk
192.168.123.222Your laptopjoin this subnet, e.g. static IP 192.168.123.222/24, before running any notebook
Hint — where to startAfter joining the subnet, `ping 192.168.123.161` and `ping 192.168.123.164` before opening any notebook — a silent `Latest` subscriber with `message is None` forever is almost always a network problem, not a code problem.
Course Intro 16 · Jupyter

Working in Jupyter notebooks

Every task in this course is a notebook cell: notebooks let you inspect live robot state between cells, and a kernel restart gives you a clean DDS re-initialization for free.

  • One ChannelFactoryInitialize call is allowed per kernel (Task 2) — restart the kernel, don't fight the guard, if you need a different interface/domain.
  • Before the native track (Tasks 2–13), warm up with the finished sdk_wrapper.G1 wrapper (task1_sdkwrapper_usage.ipynb) to see the target API surface.
from sdk_wrapper import G1

g1 = G1(iface="eth0", domain_id=0)   # one instance per kernel
g1.say("G1 academy ready.", language="EN")
g1.set_headlight(color="cyan", intensity=60, duration_s=3)
Restarting the kernel is the normal way to change iface/domain_id — ChannelFactoryInitialize refuses a silent second call with different settings.

Course Intro 19 · Using AI

Using AI as a coding aid

No specific AI CLI is required or taught in this course — but using an AI assistant (ChatGPT, Claude, or similar) to help write, explain, or debug the code you build in Tasks 2–13 is encouraged. Each task from here on includes a ready-to-copy prompt for exactly this.

  • Be specific about context. Paste the actual function signatures, topic names, and constraints you're working with — "write a G1 helper" gets a worse answer than "write ensure_channel_factory(domain_id, interface) using unitree_sdk2py.core.channel.ChannelFactoryInitialize, called at most once per process".
  • State the constraints, not just the goal. Safety rules (never invent an FSM id, always recompute the CRC, refuse stale data) belong in the prompt — an AI that doesn't know them will happily skip them.
  • Verify against the solution slide, every time. An AI-generated answer is a draft, not a source of truth — run it in your head (or in a sandbox) and compare it against this deck's solution before trusting it on the robot.
Hint — where to startA generated script is still your responsibility once it touches rt/lowcmd, rt/arm_sdk, or Dex3 command topics — the safety checklist at the end of every task applies to AI-written code exactly as much as to hand-written code.

Knowledge Task 2

Knowledge — ChannelFactory is global process state

ChannelFactoryInitialize(domain_id, interface) sets up the DDS participant for the whole process. It is not per-object, per-topic, or per-notebook-cell — it is one shared state for the entire Python process (kernel).

  • Call it exactly once, before constructing any ChannelSubscriber/ChannelPublisher.
  • Always the same (domain_id, interface) for the life of that process — a second call with different settings must not silently reconnect (that would leave half your subscribers on the old settings).
  • In Jupyter, "restart the kernel" is your reset button when you need a different interface/domain — not a workaround, the intended way.
DDS setup order: factory once, then as many publishers/subscribers as you need.
Knowledge Task 2

Knowledge — subscriber callbacks are asynchronous

A ChannelSubscriber callback runs on a background thread whenever a message arrives. Between messages, whatever you cached last time is all you have — it can be None (nothing received yet) or stale (publisher died, wrong topic/domain/interface).

  • The fix is one small class: cache the newest message + its time.time() receipt time, and expose a fresh(max_age_s) check so every later call site can refuse stale data in one line instead of repeating the staleness math.
SymptomLikely causeHow to check
message is None forevertopic name typo, wrong domain/interfaceros2 topic echo <topic> on the same network
message present, fresh() Falsepublisher stopped, robot in a mode that stops publishingcheck timestamp age vs. robot mode
fresh() flips true/false rapidlyqueue too short for a bursty publisherraise queue_len
Task Task 2

Task — build the guard and the cache

Implement two things, then use them for every subscriber for the rest of this course:

  1. ensure_channel_factory(domain_id, interface) — module-level guard: initialize once, store the config, raise on a conflicting re-call, return the stored config either way.
  2. class Latest — wraps one ChannelSubscriber; constructor takes (topic, message_type, queue_len=10), the callback stores self.message/self.timestamp, and fresh(max_age_s=0.5) returns whether the cached message exists and is recent enough.
Hint — where to startStart by subscribing to `rt/lowstate` (`unitree_hg.msg.dds_.LowState_`) — it's the topic every later task also needs, so you'll immediately be able to tell whether your guard + cache actually work.
AI Prompt Task 2

Suggested prompt

Copy this prompt to ChatGPT / Claude / your AI of choice
I'm building native DDS helpers for a Unitree G1 humanoid, using unitree_sdk2py directly
(unitree_sdk2py.core.channel: ChannelFactoryInitialize, ChannelPublisher, ChannelSubscriber).
Nothing else exists in my notebook yet.

Implement exactly these two things:

1. `ensure_channel_factory(domain_id, interface)` — a module-level guard around
   ChannelFactoryInitialize. Call it at most once per process: store the (domain_id, interface)
   the first time, call ChannelFactoryInitialize with it, and on any later call with a
   *different* (domain_id, interface) raise a RuntimeError instead of silently reconnecting.
   Return the stored config either way.

2. `class Latest` — wraps one ChannelSubscriber(topic, message_type). Constructor signature
   `__init__(self, topic, message_type, queue_len=10)`. On every callback, store the newest
   message on `self.message` and `time.time()` on `self.timestamp`. Add `fresh(self, max_age_s=0.5)`
   returning True only if `self.message is not None` and the age is within `max_age_s`.

Also add a `make_publisher(topic, message_type)` one-liner (construct + .Init(), return it) and a
`diagnose(latest, name, max_age_s=0.5)` helper that returns a human-readable string: "no message
received yet" if `latest.message is None`, otherwise "fresh"/"STALE" with the age.

Do not call ChannelFactoryInitialize more than once, and do not swallow the RuntimeError on a
conflicting re-init.
Solution Task 2

Solution — ensure_channel_factory + Latest

Full version, plus the two small helpers every later task also reuses from lib_solved.py: make_publisher and diagnose.

_factory_config = None
def ensure_channel_factory(domain_id, interface):
    global _factory_config
    config = (int(domain_id), str(interface))
    if _factory_config is None:
        ChannelFactoryInitialize(*config)
        _factory_config = config
    elif _factory_config != config:
        raise RuntimeError(f"ChannelFactory already initialized as {_factory_config}; restart kernel for {config}.")
    return _factory_config

class Latest:
    def __init__(self, topic, message_type, queue_len=10):
        self.message = None
        self.timestamp = 0.0
        self.subscriber = ChannelSubscriber(topic, message_type)
        self.subscriber.Init(self._callback, queue_len)
    def _callback(self, message):
        self.message = message
        self.timestamp = time.time()
    def fresh(self, max_age_s=0.5):
        return self.message is not None and time.time() - self.timestamp <= max_age_s

def make_publisher(topic, message_type):
    publisher = ChannelPublisher(topic, message_type)
    publisher.Init()
    return publisher

def diagnose(latest, name, max_age_s=0.5):
    if latest.message is None:
        return f"{name}: no message received yet (publisher not running / topic name wrong / domain-id or interface mismatch)"
    age = time.time() - latest.timestamp
    return f"{name}: last message {age:.2f}s ago" + (" (stale)" if age > max_age_s else " (fresh)")
Full reference: solved/task2_necessary_dds_init_pubsub.ipynb — the exact same code lives in solved/lib_solved.py under "Task 2".

Task 3 — Developing say() and set_headlight() from scratch

Builds onTask 2's ensure_channel_factory pattern, supplied in this standalone notebook by sdk_wrapper.ensure_channel_factory, plus the still-supplied util.play_piper_text boilerplate.
New in lib_solved.pyparse_color, scale_color, HeadlightThread, say, set_headlight

Same shape as sdk_wrapper.G1.say / set_headlight — you build the AudioClient plumbing, color parsing, and the cancellable thread; Piper synthesis/WAV conversion stays supplied.

Knowledge Task 3

Knowledge — AudioClient and Piper's division of labor

AudioClient is the native SDK request client for volume, LedControl, and PlayStream. Piper (a local text-to-speech engine) never talks to the robot directly — it only produces a WAV file on disk.

  • util.play_piper_text(audio_client, text, language, volume) does the tedious part (subprocess call to Piper, WAV read, mono/16-bit/16kHz resampling, PlayStream framing) so it is not something to retype.
  • You still construct+Init() the client yourself, exactly like Task 2's publisher/subscriber pattern.
  • The G1 LED RPC may return 3104 (timeout) even when it accepted the command; treat 0 and 3104 as accepted.
util.play_piper_text does the middle two steps; you own constructing/initializing the AudioClient and calling it.
Knowledge Task 3

Knowledge — color parsing and a cancellable thread

set_headlight(color, intensity, duration_s) has to accept three input shapes and hold a color for a duration — which LedControl alone cannot do (it only sets the color for a moment).

  • scale_color(rgb, intensity) scales by 0–100% before it is ever sent to LedControl.
  • Holding a color needs a background threading.Thread that calls LedControl every 0.2s until duration_s elapses or it is cancelled — and it must always try to turn the light off in a finally block, so a crash never leaves a color stuck on.
  • A new call to set_headlight must stop+join any earlier thread before starting its own — two competing threads fighting over the same LED is exactly the kind of controller-ownership bug this course keeps warning about.
Input formExampleParsed as
name"cyan"looked up in a small name→RGB table
hex"#00ffff"3 hex byte pairs
csv"0,255,255"3 clamped ints

Implement:

1. `say(text, language="en", volume=100)` — construct/Init() an AudioClient once at module scope,
   call `util.play_piper_text` with it.

2. `parse_color(value)` — accept a color name from a small dict (white/red/green/blue/yellow/cyan/
   magenta/orange/purple/pink), a `#RRGGBB` hex string, or an `"R,G,B"` string; return a clamped
   `(r, g, b)` int tuple in all three cases; raise ValueError otherwise.

3. `scale_color(rgb, intensity)` — scale each channel by `intensity` (0-100%).

4. `class HeadlightThread(threading.Thread)` — takes `(audio_client, rgb, duration_s, interval_s,
   stop_event)`. `run()` calls `audio_client.LedControl(*rgb)` every `interval_s` seconds until
   `stop_event` is set or `duration_s` elapses, and ALWAYS attempts `LedControl(0, 0, 0)` in a
   `finally` block so a crash never leaves a color stuck on.

5. `set_headlight(color="green", intensity=100, duration_s=3)` — one immediate LedControl call; if
   `duration_s > 0`, stop+join any previously running HeadlightThread before starting a new one.

Requirement: a second call to `set_headlight` while a thread from an earlier call is still alive
must stop and join that earlier thread before starting its own.
Solution Task 3

Solution — the cancellable headlight thread

The part worth seeing in full is the thread; say/parse_color/scale_color are short helpers around supplied pieces. The deployed G1 may return 3104 after accepting an LED command, so it is handled like 0.

def led_control_was_accepted(code):
    return int(code) in (0, 3104)

class HeadlightThread(threading.Thread):
    def __init__(self, audio_client, rgb, duration_s, interval_s, stop_event):
        super().__init__(daemon=False)
        self.audio_client, self.rgb = audio_client, rgb
        self.duration_s = max(0.0, float(duration_s))
        self.interval_s = max(0.0, float(interval_s))
        self.stop_event = stop_event
    def run(self):
        end_time = time.monotonic() + self.duration_s
        try:
            while not self.stop_event.is_set() and time.monotonic() < end_time:
                code = int(self.audio_client.LedControl(*self.rgb))
                if not led_control_was_accepted(code):
                    self.stop_event.set(); break
                self.stop_event.wait(self.interval_s)
        finally:
            try: self.audio_client.LedControl(0, 0, 0)      # always attempt off
            except Exception: pass

def set_headlight(color="green", intensity=100, duration_s=3):
    global _headlight_stop, _headlight_thread
    rgb = scale_color(parse_color(color), intensity)
    if _headlight_thread is not None and _headlight_thread.is_alive():
        _headlight_stop.set(); _headlight_thread.join()      # stop+join before starting a new one
    code = int(audio_client.LedControl(*rgb))
    if not led_control_was_accepted(code) or float(duration_s) <= 0:
        return code
    _headlight_stop = threading.Event()
    _headlight_thread = HeadlightThread(audio_client, rgb, duration_s, 0.2, _headlight_stop)
    _headlight_thread.start()
    return code

Knowledge Task 4

Knowledge — defensive reads and map validation

Two patterns worth internalizing here, because you will reuse both for the rest of the course.

  • Defensive attribute access: SportModeState_ field names vary a little across SDK/firmware versions (position vs. pos vs. position_w). A small _first_attr(obj, names, default) helper tries each candidate name in order instead of assuming one exact spelling — the same defensive pattern sdk_wrapper.py uses internally.
  • Refuse instead of guess: academy/todo.txt flags the occupancy-grid topic/type as unconfirmed. get_occupancygrid() raises NotImplementedError with instructions rather than wiring a guessed topic/type pair that could silently return wrong or empty data. A loud, documented gap beats a quiet, wrong answer.
Hint — where to startConfirm the real occupancy-grid topic with `ros2 topic list` / `ros2 topic info -v` against the running SLAM stack before ever removing that NotImplementedError.

Solution Task 4

Solution — lowstate, odom, and the refusal

The three shortest, most-reused readers. Battery/SLAM/RGBD/services follow the same shape — see lib_solved.py for all seven.

def get_lowstate():
    msg = lowstate_sub.message
    if msg is None: return None
    motors, imu = list(msg.motor_state), msg.imu_state
    return {"timestamp": lowstate_sub.timestamp,
            "joint_positions": [float(m.q) for m in motors],
            "joint_velocities": [float(m.dq) for m in motors],
            "joint_torques": [float(m.tau_est) for m in motors],
            "imu": {"rpy": [float(imu.rpy[i]) for i in range(3)],
                    "gyro": [float(imu.gyroscope[i]) for i in range(3)],
                    "acc": [float(imu.accelerometer[i]) for i in range(3)]}}

def _first_attr(obj, names, default=None):
    for name in names:
        if hasattr(obj, name): return getattr(obj, name)
    return default

def get_odommodestate():
    msg = odom_sub.message
    if msg is None: return None
    position = _first_attr(msg, ("position", "pos", "position_w"))
    return {"timestamp": odom_sub.timestamp,
            "position": None if position is None else tuple(float(x) for x in position),
            "gait_type": _first_attr(msg, ("gait_type", "gaitType", "gait"))}

def get_occupancygrid():
    raise NotImplementedError(
        "Confirm the deployed occupancy-grid topic/message type against the "
        "running SLAM stack before implementing this; do not guess.")
Solution Task 4

Solution — battery source priority

Battery is the clearest example of "try the dedicated source, fall back only if it's stale" — a pattern you'll see again in Task 7's SLAM pose.

BMS_TOPICS = ["rt/lf/bmsstate", "rt/lf/agvbmsstate", "rt/bmsstate", "rt/agvbmsstate"]
bms_subs = [(topic, Latest(topic, msg_type)) for topic in BMS_TOPICS for msg_type in _bms_types()]

def get_battery():
    for topic, sub in bms_subs:
        if sub.fresh(max_age_s=3.0):                 # dedicated topic, still fresh
            msg = sub.message
            return {"source": topic, "soc": int(msg.soc), "current": int(msg.current), "cycle": int(msg.cycle)}
    msg = lowstate_sub.message                        # fallback: embedded in lowstate
    if msg is None: return None
    return {"source": "rt/lowstate",
            "power_v": None if getattr(msg, "power_v", None) is None else float(msg.power_v),
            "power_a": None if getattr(msg, "power_a", None) is None else float(msg.power_a)}
